The internal structures proper to the cothurnia, i.e. the zooid, are gilded with a translucent or loricous tubular envelope characteristic of it. This loric ends with a short peduncle by which the cothurnia attaches itself during the so-called vegetative or sessile phase of its existence, to the surface of a variety of hosts (crustaceous, fish, polychaetes, aquatic plants, etc.). This type of non-invasive and opportunistic attachment to the external substrate of live hosts is an example of an epibiotic relationship. Measurements of abundance of epibiont cothurnia on the surface of chevrettes (freshwater shrimps) serve as a valuable environmental index to determine freshwater quality, as these ciliates are extremely sensitive to the deterioration of the latter.
